summaries.example: Imagine a basket of fruit. One group is all the apples, and another group is all the bananas. Joining the groups makes a bigger group; finding what they share means taking an intersection; choosing everything that is not in a group means taking its complement. With only two truth values, 0 can mean false and 1 can mean true.
summaries.summary: Boolean algebra is a way to study systems with two-valued choices. Its basic example uses sets. You can join sets with union, find their shared part with intersection, and take the complement of a set. The same patterns describe the logic of “or,” “and,” and “not.” In the smallest Boolean algebra, 0 means false and 1 means true. Mathematicians define Boolean algebras by rules that make these operations behave consistently. They can then ask what all such systems have in common. Some have atoms, or smallest nonzero pieces, while atomless algebras do not. A partial order also lets mathematicians say when one element is below another. The subject connects algebra with logic, sets, topology, measure, and other areas of mathematics.
key_ideas: Boolean algebra uses rules for combining things and for handling two-valued logic.
The simplest Boolean algebra has just 0 and 1, which can stand for false and true.
Sets give a concrete picture: union acts like “or,” intersection like “and,” and complement like “not.”
Boolean algebras can be studied as algebraic systems, collections of sets, or tools connected with logic and computer circuits.
Some Boolean algebras have atoms, while atomless ones have no smallest nonzero pieces.
A Boolean algebra is complete when every collection of its elements has both the needed least upper bound and greatest lower bound.
summaries.why_it_matters: Boolean algebra gives one clear language for patterns found in logic, sets, and two-choice systems. It helps mathematicians recognize when different-looking problems have the same structure. The source also shows that Boolean algebras connect to topics such as switching circuits, computer-like reasoning, topology, and the foundations of mathematics.

important_terms.definition: A mathematical system for working with two choices, such as true and false or belonging and not belonging.
A collection of objects treated as one group. In Boolean algebra, sets can be joined, compared, and changed to their complements.
Putting two sets together to make one set containing everything in either set.
The part shared by two sets: the objects that belong to both.
The objects in the larger universe that are not in a chosen set.
A smallest building piece in a Boolean algebra: it is not zero and has no smaller nonzero piece below it.

questions_to_think_about: Where do you use choices like yes/no or on/off in everyday life?
How is “or” like putting two groups together?
Could a group have no smallest pieces? What might that mean?
Why might mathematicians want different pictures of the same structure?

summaries.example: Suppose a theory contains statements built from sentence letters using “or,” “and,” and “not.” Treat two formulas as the same when the theory proves that they are equivalent. The equivalence classes of formulas can be combined using those three connectives, producing a Boolean algebra. This is a Lindenbaum-Tarski algebra: logical relationships become algebraic structure.
summaries.summary: The mathematics of Boolean algebra studies an abstract algebraic structure modeled by sets under union, intersection, and complementation and by two-valued logic under disjunction, conjunction, and negation. Its axioms support a natural partial order: in the set model, this is inclusion. The two-element algebra is especially important because an equation holds in all Boolean algebras exactly when it holds there. Boolean algebras can be recast as idempotent rings, so the subject belongs to standard algebra as well as logic. The source develops ideals, filters, ultrafilters, homomorphisms, completions, free algebras, and special classes such as atomic, atomless, complete, interval, tree, and superatomic algebras. Stone representation shows that every Boolean algebra has a concrete set representation based on ultrafilters and corresponds to a certain kind of topological space. Deeper structural questions use cardinal functions measuring disjointness, independence, density, and related features. The source also distinguishes decidable from undecidable theories and explains how formulas modulo logical equivalence form Lindenbaum-Tarski algebras. Finally, complete Boolean algebras can provide the values in Boolean-valued models, including models used in set theory.
key_ideas: The set-theoretic and two-element examples motivate an axiomatic theory: Boolean algebras are not merely collections of sets, but abstract algebras obeying the same laws.
Every equation true in the two-element Boolean algebra is true in every Boolean algebra, and conversely.
Boolean algebras can also be described through idempotent rings, showing a precise equivalence between two algebraic presentations.
Stone representation connects every Boolean algebra with an algebra of sets and with a totally disconnected compact Hausdorff space.
Structure theory studies properties such as atoms, independence, cellularity, density, incomparability, and rigidity.

The elementary theory of Boolean algebras is decidable, while adding a distinguished subalgebra produces an undecidable theory; adding a distinguished ideal remains decidable in the result described by the source.
summaries.why_it_matters: Boolean algebra shows how one structure can unify logic, algebra, set theory, topology, and model theory. It clarifies why truth-table reasoning can be studied with algebraic methods and why logical equivalence classes can themselves form mathematical objects. Its representation theorems also connect abstract rules with concrete sets and spaces, while its decidability results show that small changes in the language can affect what can be mechanically determined.

important_terms.definition: An algebraic structure with union-like, intersection-like, and complement-like operations satisfying laws corresponding to two-valued logic.
The relation x ≤ y defined by x + y = y; for sets, it corresponds to subset inclusion.
A nonzero element with no element strictly between it and zero. An atomic algebra places an atom below every nonzero element.
A Boolean algebra in which every collection of elements has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound.
A map preserving the relevant algebraic operations. An isomorphism is a structure-preserving correspondence in both directions.
The theorem representing a Boolean algebra as an algebra of sets of ultrafilters, with algebraic operations represented by set operations.
The theory of a class is decidable when there is an effective method for determining whether its statements are true in that class.
The Boolean algebra formed from formulas or sentences by identifying those equivalent under a theory, then interpreting logical connectives algebraically.

questions_to_think_about: Why can the two-element algebra test all equations of Boolean algebras?
What is gained by representing an abstract algebra as sets or as a topological space?
Why might adding a distinguished subalgebra change a theory from decidable to undecidable?
How does identifying logically equivalent formulas turn logic into algebra?
What could it mean for a Boolean algebra to be rigid, with only the identity automorphism?

summaries.example: Think of a school club’s activities. Let A be the students who joined the art activity and B the students who joined the music activity. A union B means students in at least one activity; A intersection B means students in both; the complement of A means students not in art. These same operations can be read as “or,” “and,” and “not.” A Boolean algebra studies the rules that make these operations work, even when its elements are not literally sets.
summaries.summary: Boolean algebra studies a mathematical pattern shared by sets and two-valued logic. In a set model, union, intersection, and complement correspond to “or,” “and,” and “not.” The subject defines these patterns abstractly through algebraic laws, so the elements need not be sets. A partial order describes when one element is below another, and the two-element algebra gives the values false and true. An important result says that an equation is valid in every Boolean algebra exactly when it is valid in this two-element example. The source also explains atoms, completeness, ideals, filters, ultrafilters, and maps between algebras. Stone’s representation theorem connects Boolean algebras with algebras of sets and with a class of topological spaces. Different special classes reveal different structures: atomless algebras have no smallest nonzero parts, while superatomic algebras have a particularly strong atomic behavior. Cardinal functions compare large or infinite features, such as families of disjoint or independent elements. Finally, Boolean algebra connects directly to logic through Lindenbaum-Tarski algebras, where logically equivalent formulas are grouped together. The source distinguishes the decidable theory of Boolean algebras from nearby theories that are undecidable, and introduces Boolean-valued models for set theory.
key_ideas: Boolean algebra gives an abstract version of set operations and two-valued logic.
The two-element algebra acts as a basic test case for equations in all Boolean algebras.
Ultrafilters help represent an abstract Boolean algebra as a concrete algebra of sets, and this leads to a connection with topology.
Boolean algebras come in important kinds, including atomic, atomless, complete, interval, tree, and superatomic algebras.
Mathematicians compare algebras using structural measurements such as cellularity, independence, density, and incomparability.
The logical theory of Boolean algebras is decidable, but related theories can become undecidable when extra structure is named.
summaries.why_it_matters: This subject teaches a powerful mathematical lesson: the same pattern can appear in different settings and still be studied with the same rules. Boolean algebra helps connect everyday ideas about groups and choices with formal logic, abstract algebra, topology, and set theory. It also raises important questions about representation, proof, and the boundary between problems that can and cannot be solved by a general procedure.

important_terms.definition: An abstract algebra whose operations follow the same basic patterns as union, intersection, and taking a complement.
A relationship that arranges elements from lower to higher; in the set example, one set is below another when it is a subset.
A filter that makes a complete yes-or-no choice for every element: it contains the element or its complement, but not zero.
A result saying that every Boolean algebra can be represented using sets built from its ultrafilters.
A Boolean algebra with no atoms, meaning no nonzero element is a smallest piece.
A way to measure or describe features of a Boolean algebra, such as how many disjoint or independent elements it can have.
A theory is decidable when a method can determine whether each statement in it is true; undecidable means no such general method exists.
An algebra made by treating logically equivalent sentences as the same and matching algebraic operations with logical connectives.

questions_to_think_about: Why might the same operation be understood both as a set operation and as a logical connective?
What does an ultrafilter’s all-or-nothing choice tell us about a Boolean algebra?
How can an algebra be infinite but still have atoms?
Why could naming a subalgebra make questions harder to decide than naming an ideal?
What are the benefits and limits of representing an abstract object in a different mathematical language?
